title: Venus Williams Lands US Open Wildcard — Will Serena Join the Party?
summary:
Venus Williams is heading to the US Open again — and this time, her sister Serena might be right behind her. Venus, now 46, received a wildcard into the singles main draw, which kicks off on August 30 in New York. It's a tournament she knows well: she first played there 29 years ago as a teenager, reached the final in her debut in 1997, and won the title in 2000 and 2001.

But the big question on everyone's mind: will Serena join her? Serena, 44, made her comeback to tennis in June after a four-year hiatus. She played singles at Wimbledon but injured her knee in her first-round match. The sisters were supposed to play doubles together at Wimbledon but had to pull out. They finally reunited on the doubles court in Cincinnati on Tuesday, losing a nail-biter in three sets. The crowd went wild just to see them together again.

There's still one wildcard spot left for the singles draw, and fans are hoping Serena gets it. She's a 23-time Grand Slam champion, and her return has been one of the biggest stories in tennis this year.

Venus, though, has struggled in singles lately. She's lost all 10 of her matches this season and hasn't won a singles match since July 2025. But she's always a crowd favorite, and she's done well in doubles recently, reaching the quarter-finals at the US Open last year with Leylah Fernandez.

The Williams sisters have always drawn huge crowds, whether together or apart. Their return in Cincinnati packed the stands. If Serena gets that wildcard, the US Open could be the stage for another epic Williams moment.
why_it_matters: This story shows how sports leagues balance fairness and star power, and how athletes can remain valuable to their sport even after their peak years. For young people, the Williams sisters are an example of longevity, reinvention, and the pull of legacy.

background_read: Venus Williams and her younger sister Serena Williams grew up in Compton, California, and were coached by their father Richard Williams; both became famous for their power and athleticism and are widely regarded as legends of tennis.
Venus turned professional as a teenager in the 1990s, while Serena is considered one of the greatest tennis players in history and holds the 23 Grand Slam championships mentioned in the article.
The US Open is one of the four Grand Slam tournaments, held annually in New York on hard courts, and it is the final major of the tennis season.

Wildcards are special invitations that let tournament organizers add players whose ranking would not otherwise qualify them, often for past champions, crowd favorites, or players returning from injury.

The Cincinnati event mentioned in the article is the Western & Southern Open, a major hard-court tournament that many players use as a final tune-up before the US Open and that has hosted the Williams sisters in both singles and doubles over their careers.

perspectives.description: Fans and tournament organizers gain from the Williams sisters' unmatched star power. Their matches fill stadiums and attract viewers who might not otherwise watch the early rounds, which can boost revenue and visibility for women's tennis.

Critics may question whether a player who has lost all 10 singles matches this season should receive a wildcard over younger or higher-ranked competitors. That concern is about merit and whether wildcards should go to players in stronger current form.

Wildcards have always been a tool for balancing competitive merit with commercial and historical appeal. Venus's entry shows how tournaments weigh legacy, crowd appeal, and past achievement alongside recent results.

If Serena receives the remaining singles wildcard, the US Open could become a symbolic final act for the Williams era. That could influence how Grand Slams market veteran athletes and create pathways for other returning champions.
